On Language Drift during RLVR Post-Training

Michael Sullivan Affiliation: Department of Language Science and Technology, Saarland University, Saarbrücken, Germany Correspondence to: msullivan@lst.uni-saarland.de    Alexander Koller Affiliation: Department of Language Science and Technology, Saarland University, Saarbrücken, Germany
Abstract

Recent advances in LLM reasoning models—driven primarily by the paradigm of post-training via reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR)—have enabled them to accomplish impressively complex tasks. However, in parallel with their rising capabilities, LLMs have increasingly displayed signs of language drift in their chains of thought (CoTs): unusual, non-standard, and seemingly nonsensical language use. Although it is well-documented—and can potentially impair CoT monitorability—the causes of language drift are thus far poorly understood. In this paper, we identify the conditions under which language drift occurs: we prove theoretically that RLVR optimization pressure permits unbounded language drift, while supervised fine-tuning does not. We then show empirically that language drift specifically arises during RLVR on novel reasoning tasks—i.e. when the target behavior cannot be drawn out of the base model. Finally, we prove that it is not possible to constrain language drift without constraining expected reward, suggesting that CoT monitorability cannot be improved without harming performance during RLVR post-training at the frontier.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Recent, drastic gains in the reasoning capabilities of frontier models have enabled LLM-based agents to solve increasingly complex, long-horizon coding tasks (Huang et al., 2026), solve long-standing mathematical problems (Alon et al., 2026, e.g.), etc. These impressive and rapid improvements have been driven primarily by scaling reinforcement learning (RL; OpenAI, 2024; Guo et al., 2025, etc.)—in particular, reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR), which optimizes for deterministic, outcome-based rewards such as final-answer correctness.

However, frontier LLMs have simultaneously been displaying increasing degrees of language drift: novel linguistic behavior that is non-standard and/or ungrammatical—and occasionally illegible—to human readers (Lazaridou et al., 2020). As an example, the RLVR-trained model in Figure 1 has undergone language drift, affecting not only the style of its reasoning trace, but also the interpretation of the reference (meaning) of the terms that it uses. In particular, it conflates the cost of the dog—which is not relevant or stated—with the cost of the grooming.

Language drift is naturally frustrating to users, who struggle to parse the atypical constructions and idiosyncratic vocabulary use displayed by LLM agents. The ubiquity and severity of this problem are such that attempted workarounds have become frequent topics of online discussion: skills11 1 e.g. https://github.com/danyuchn/asd-ste100-skill. instructing models to use only ASD-STE100 Simplified Technical English, “Claudish-to-English translators” (see Figure 2), etc.

Beyond user frustration with difficult prose, more extreme degrees of language drift (see e.g. Figure 3) pose a more serious threat in the form of decreased chain of thought (CoT) monitorability (Baker et al., 2025; Korbak et al., 2025): illegible CoTs—either to humans or other LLMs—render models’ internal reasoning processes more opaque, leading to difficulty in determining intent and predicting future actions. This consequence of language drift is particularly worrisome in light of safety concerns due to recent security incidents involving unintended LLM agent behavior22 2 e.g. the OpenAI Hugging Face hacking incident..

Despite its prevalence and potential consequences, the reasons for language drift remain poorly understood. Although RLVR has been suggested as a potential culprit (Korbak et al., 2025), it has thus far been unclear whether language drift can occur purely due to RLVR optimization pressure. In this paper, we answer this question in the affirmative: namely, we prove theoretically that RLVR training alone permits unbounded language drift, while supervised fine-tuning (SFT) prevents language drift beyond a fixed, finite upper bound (see Figure 1; Section 4).

We additionally prove in Section 4 that constraining language drift necessarily constrains reward, in the sense that limiting the degree of language drift that an LLM can undergo during RLVR training limits the maximum expected reward that the model can attain. This result supports arguments that maintaining CoT monitorability may not be possible without hindering downstream performance (Baker et al., 2025, e.g.).

We then investigate the precise cause of language drift. We argue that language drift is simply a special case of novel behavior—namely, novel linguistic behavior. Given that novel behavior arises during RLVR when behavior sharpening—drawing target reasoning behavior out of the base model—is not possible (Liu et al., 2025), we hypothesize that language drift occurs as a side-effect of novel behavior discovery during RLVR on novel tasks. In Section 5, we provide empirical evidence in support of this hypothesis, demonstrating that when behavior sharpening is not possible, models display greater degrees of language drift during RLVR than during SFT.

We further provide evidence that different RLVR training runs starting from the same model—and trained on the same dataset—develop distinct linguistic behavior: i.e. each RLVR training run undergoes unique language drift. A potential consequence of this finding is that even models trained on the same tasks may not be able to monitor the CoTs of an LLM that has undergone sufficient language drift.

Taken together, these findings paint a troubling picture of the future balance between LLM safety and capability. Namely, language drift occurs during RLVR on novel reasoning tasks—precisely those tasks which must be conquered to advance the frontier—and cannot be constrained without harming expected performance. This conclusion raises the question: as frontier models advance to human-level capability and beyond, will it remain possible to monitor their reasoning traces in order to verify alignment?

2 Related Work

Language Drift during RL.

LLMs often exhibit nonsensical linguistic patterns under RLHF-style (Ouyang et al., 2022) optimization pressure: for example, models can learn to repeatedly generate the same token when using rewards derived from a neural sentiment-analysis classifier (Korbak et al., 2022). While this certainly qualifies as language drift in the narrowest sense, we exclude such reward-hacking-like phenomena from our analysis, and focus instead on the development of novel—but internally coherent—linguistic behavior.

To that end, Mordatch and Abbeel (2018) study the emergence of communicative behavior resembling language during multi-agent RL with a limited action space and simple, RNN-based agents initialized from scratch. They find that goal-based reward provides sufficient optimization pressure for these agents to invent language-like, compositional communication codes over an abstract set of symbols. Similarly, Lazaridou et al. (2020) observe language drift—including shifting word meanings—when training LSTM-based (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, 1997) language models to play referential games via multi-agent RL.

These studies demonstrate that RL optimization pressure can cause linguistic invention in settings targeting communication ability. Our results in Section 5 extend these findings to more general and widely used reasoning settings, and to modern transformer architectures and RLVR algorithms.

Illegible Reasoning Traces.

Guo et al. (2025) report that DeepSeek-R1-Zero exhibits ‘‘poor readability and language mixing’’33 3 It is unclear to what degree language mixing represents genuine language drift in the sense of Definition 1, as language mixing is also well-documented in bilingual human language users (Poplack, 1980, in the form of code-switching; see e.g.)., in particular switching between English and Chinese. Although adding a language-specific penalty improves readability, it harms performance: this finding is consistent with our theoretical result in Section 4.2 (Theorem 3) that language drift cannot be constrained without negatively impacting expected reward.

Jose (2025) finds that frontier reasoning models sometimes output illegible and (seemingly) nonsensical CoTs within otherwise valid reasoning traces. Furthermore, removing these illegible portions of the reasoning traces considerably harms performance, suggesting that although the text may be nonsensical to human readers, it is still useful for—and therefore legible to—the LLM. Panfilov et al. (2026) similarly find human-illegible text in frontier models’ internal reasoning traces.

Our theoretical and empirical findings in Sections 4-5 shed light on these results demonstrating language drift in SoTA, RLVR-trained reasoning models. In particular, our results suggest that this observed language drift arose during RLVR post-training on novel reasoning tasks.

Inducing Novel Linguistic Behavior.

Vaduguru et al. (2026) use DPO-style preference optimization (Rafailov et al., 2023) to train LLMs to perform ad-hoc linguistic convention formation in multi-turn dialog settings. Although these authors deliberately pressure LLMs to develop unique linguistic behavior, their objective is efficiency in agent-human communication, and their training method therefore cannot induce (nor does it target) arbitrary language drift.

Zhu et al. (2026) use prompting-based methods to compress text into human-illegible form—without substantially impacting its LLM-legibility—in order to condense models’ context windows without information loss. While this method merely elicits language drift potential already present in the model (as it relies purely on prompting), it demonstrates that LLMs do not necessarily need to operate over human-legible language.

3 Preliminaries

We focus our analysis in this work on text-based reasoning LLMs: models that produce a CoT and an answer, given a prompt. We deliberately exclude multimodal models for the sake of analytical tractability, and leave an investigation of such models to future work.

As such, we treat an LLM as a conditional probability distribution π{\pi} over 𝒵×𝒴\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Y} given 𝒳\mathcal{X}—i.e. over pairs (z,y)(z,y) of CoTs zz and answers yy, given a prompt xx.

We define P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}} to be a joint distribution over 𝒳×𝒵×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Y}, in order to permit direct comparison with π{\pi}.

Computing P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}} is of course in practice intractable, and we do not aim to do so here: our analysis simply treats P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}} as an unknown—but fixed—point in probability space. We permit the possibility that P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}} is derived from an underlying, context-conditioned distribution ℙ(HL)\mathbb{P}^{(\textit{HL})}: for example, in the context of math reasoning tasks, we may assume that P(HL)=ℙ(HL)​(–|task=math-reasoning){P^{(\textit{HL})}}=\mathbb{P}^{(\textit{HL})}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\textit{task}=\textit{math-reasoning}).

In order to theoretically analyze the respective behavior of SFT and RLVR training with respect to language drift, it is first necessary to formally model the notions of SFT and RLVR training runs.

3.3 Assumptions

We make a few mild assumptions throughout this work in order to simplify the proofs of Theorems 1-3. First, we assume that P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}, D(SFT){{D}^{(\textit{SFT})}}, and all models π\pi have full support on 𝒳×𝒵×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Y}, and that D(RL){{D}^{(\textit{RL})}} has full support on 𝒳×𝒴\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{Y}. We assume further that D(RL)​(–|x){{D}^{(\textit{RL})}}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx) is not uniform for every x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}.

We additionally assume a finite vocabulary size and finite prompt, CoT, and answer lengths ℓ𝒳,ℓ𝒵,ℓ𝒴\ell_{\mathcal{X}},\ell_{\mathcal{Z}},\ell_{\mathcal{Y}} (respectively). This assumption reflects the reality of LLMs with finite token vocabularies and finite context windows. All proofs are valid for any choice of ℓ𝒳,ℓ𝒵,ℓ𝒴≥1\ell_{\mathcal{X}},\ell_{\mathcal{Z}},\ell_{\mathcal{Y}}\geq 1.

4 When Does Language Drift Occur?

4.1 RLVR Permits Language Drift, SFT Does Not

We prove that SFT optimization pressure results in a finite upper bound on the degree of possible language drift that a model can undergo (Theorem 2), while RLVR optimization does not carry such an upper bound (Theorem 1). Although Korbak et al. (2025) informally hypothesize that RLVR may no longer incentivize legibility, Theorems 1-2 represent, to the best of our knowledge, the first formal proofs that RLVR permits unbounded language drift, while SFT does not.

Informally, RLVR permits unbounded language drift because this training regimen maximizes only the probability of producing a correct answer yy for a given prompt xx. Critically, the conditional πn(RL)​(𝒵|𝒳)\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{n}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X}) can drift arbitrarily far from P(HL)​(𝒵|𝒳){P^{(\textit{HL})}}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X}), without negatively altering the expected reward: it is precisely this potentially unbounded KL drift in the variable 𝒵\mathcal{Z} which drives potentially unbounded language drift across the board.

Theorem 1.

For any choice of P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}, π0(RL)\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{0}, and D(RL){{D}^{(\textit{RL})}} under the assumptions in Section 3.3:

supπ0(RL),…,πn(RL)​LD⁡(πn(RL))=∞\underset{\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{0},\dots,\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{n}}{\sup}\operatorname{LD}(\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{n})=\infty

Where supπ0(RL),…,πn(RL)\underset{\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{0},\dots,\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{n}}{\sup} denotes the supremum over all RLVR checkpoint families over D(RL){{D}^{(\textit{RL})}} initialized with π0(RL)\pi^{(\textit{RL})}_{0}.

As a consequence of Theorem 2, no SFT run can exceed a fixed degree γ\gamma of drift from the human language distribution P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}} while still minimizing cross-entropy with the target distribution D(SFT){{D}^{(\textit{SFT})}}.

4.2 Constraining Language Drift Constrains Expected Reward

We now prove that language drift cannot be constrained during RLVR training without limiting expected reward. Specifically, Theorem 3 states that for every language drift radius ϵ\epsilon around P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}, there is a larger radius δ>ϵ\delta>\epsilon which permits a greater expected reward than ϵ\epsilon (see Figure 4).

Conceptually, this is because the optimal policy—the distribution π∗{\pi}^{*} that maximizes the expected reward defined in Equation 2—concentrates all of its conditional probability mass on a single point: the most-likely answer y∗=argmaxy⁡D(RL)​(y|x)y^{*}=\operatorname{argmax}_{y}{{D}^{(\textit{RL})}}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx) for a given prompt xx. Although the KL divergence driving language drift in Theorem 3 can result entirely from shifting probability mass in the answer distribution π⁡(𝒴|𝒳,𝒵){\pi}(\mathcal{Y}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Z})—and therefore does not necessitate change in the CoT distribution π⁡(𝒵|𝒳){\pi}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X})—altering π⁡(𝒴|𝒳,𝒵){\pi}(\mathcal{Y}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Z}) while holding π⁡(𝒵|𝒳){\pi}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X}) constant still undeniably constitutes language drift.

To illustrate this point, consider a frontier-level task D(RL){{D}^{(\textit{RL})}} that humans struggle to solve: in such a case, P(HL)​(𝒵,𝒴|𝒳){P^{(\textit{HL})}}(\mathcal{Z},\mathcal{Y}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X}) by definition concentrates probability mass on incorrect trace/answer pairs (z−,y−)(z_{-},y_{-}). If π{\pi} were to increase expected reward without substantial drift in π⁡(𝒵|𝒳){\pi}(\mathcal{Z}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526pt\mathcal{X}), then π{\pi} would necessarily produce pairs of incorrect traces z−z_{-} followed by correct answers y+y_{+}, which implies that the interpretation of the trace z−z_{-} has drifted substantially from its original meaning.

It follows from Theorem 3 that during RLVR post-training, as maximum expected reward approaches supπℛ⁡(D(RL),π)\sup_{\pi}{\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},{\pi}), minimum possible language drift approaches infinity (see Figure 5). As a consequence, it is not possible to prevent language drift while also maximizing expected reward: constraining language drift to a fixed degree necessarily constrains the maximum possible expected reward that can be achieved. This result may therefore explain existing empirical evidence indicating that linguistic regularization harms performance on reasoning tasks (Guo et al., 2025, see e.g.).

4.3 Hypothesis: Novel Tasks Induce Language Drift

Theorem 1 implies that RLVR permits a given training run to undergo an arbitrary degree of language drift, while continuing to maximize expected reward. Theorem 3 goes further, and states that language drift must occur to maximize expected reward.

These theorems do not, however, establish the degree of language drift that must occur during practical RLVR training: for some task/model pairs, it is likely the case that only a minimal amount of language drift is required to achieve a practically acceptable expected reward. In other words, we do not establish the (likely task-dependent) steepness of the curve in Figure 5.

As such, it is entirely possible that some SFT run undergoes a higher degree of language drift than an RLVR training run on the same task. The point is rather that the maximum possible language drift that an RLVR training run can undergo is unbounded, and therefore greater than the maximum of an SFT run.

This is to say that while RLVR provides a setting in which language drift can arise, it does not in itself cause language drift to occur. In fact, RL’s Razor (Shenfeld et al., 2026) posits that RL prefers to find solutions with minimal KL divergence to the base model, which seemingly suggests that RLVR tends to not lead to language drift. This aligns with recent findings that RLVR simply sharpens distributions, i.e. only draws out reasoning patterns already present in the base model (Yue et al., 2025).

However, Liu et al. (2025) find that LLMs can in fact develop novel behavior under RLVR, when training on novel reasoning tasks. We argue that—absent optimization pressure on the CoT zz—those same pressures driving novel behavior development similarly increase the likelihood that novel linguistic behavior (i.e. language drift) arises: we hypothesize that language drift occurs as a side-effect of novel behavior discovery during RLVR over novel reasoning tasks.

Conversely, we argue that language drift does not occur when the targeted reasoning task is not novel to the model: by definition, a non-novel task can be solved by drawing behavior out of the base model (behavior sharpening). In this case, RL’s Razor implies that the lowest-KL path—behavior sharpening—will be preferred, and therefore no meaningful language drift will occur.

5 Experiments

We first aim to demonstrate empirically our theoretical findings in Section 4.1 that RLVR permits greater language drift than SFT. Our second objective is to validate our hypothesis laid out in Section 4.3 that novel tasks in particular induce language drift in the context of RLVR training.

To that end, we study three models using the GSM8K math reasoning dataset (Cobbe et al., 2021): gemma-3-1b-pt44 4 https://huggingface.co/google/gemma-3-1b-pt (Kamath et al., 2025), Llama-3.2-1B55 5 https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), and Qwen2.5-1.5B66 6 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B (Yang et al., 2025). We strictly limit our experiments to base models, in order to avoid potential confounding factors arising from dataset contamination during mid- and/or post-training. In addition, the use of poorly performing base models allows us to use a simple—and therefore computationally inexpensive—task to emulate a difficult, novel task, while furthermore having annotated reasoning traces available for SFT tuning.

We make all code used in these experiments available on GitHub77 7 https://github.com/coli-saar/language-drift.

5.1 Methodology

To evaluate the difference in language drift between SFT and RLVR, we trained the base models using both training methods. We employed the DAPO (Yu et al., 2025) variant of GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) as our RLVR implementation.

5.1.1 Training and Validation

For all three models, we first performed RLVR and SFT hyperparameter grid searches to identify the best-performing configuration for each training method (further details are located in Appendix B.1). We then replicated the optimal-hyperparameter run for each model and training method across five random seeds, for a total of 30 training runs.

During training and validation, the models were prompted with two fixed few-shot examples (see Figure 8 in the Appendix). During validation and RLVR training, we limited the models to 256 generated tokens. Answers were submitted using the format “####{ANSWER}”, and we extracted the final answer detected in the model’s response to compute reward/correctness.

Iso-Performance Checkpoint Selection.

For each training run, we selected for evaluation the highest-scoring checkpoint on a validation set of 128 withheld examples. However, the Llama and Gemma SFT runs consistently outperformed their RLVR counterparts. To control for any possible confounding relationship between final validation performance and language drift, we additionally selected the checkpoint from each SFT run with the closest validation score to that of the RLVR run for the same model and seed: we refer to these checkpoints as iso-SFT during evaluation.

On the other hand, the Qwen RLVR checkpoints consistently outperformed SFT: we therefore also selected the checkpoint from each Qwen RLVR run with the closest validation score to that of the Qwen SFT run with the same seed (iso-RLVR).

Behavior-Sharpening Detection.

As discussed above, we extracted the final submitted answer for validation and RLVR training reward. However, as base models, all three untrained LLMs failed to stop after emitting an answer to the prompted question; instead, they simply continued generating in-distribution question/trace/answer triples until the length limit was reached.

As such, we computed accuracy for the base LLMs relative to both the first and last submitted answer, in order to obtain a rough estimate of the models’ propensity for behavior sharpening: if an LLM has a high first-submitted answer accuracy and a low last-submitted answer accuracy, then to achieve a high reward, it needs only learn to emit the EOS token after submitting the answer (rather than generate another question). In this case, the model clearly does not need to discover new behavior, and so RLVR can solve the task primarily through behavior sharpening.

5.1.2 Evaluation

As discussed in Section 3, we do not have access to the human language distribution P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}. As such, it is not possible to directly measure language drift in these experiments. We instead use three instruct models to approximate P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}: Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct88 8 https://huggingface.co/meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct99 9 https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct, and OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct1010 10 https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct (Walsh et al., 2024).

Although by our own arguments made throughout this paper, all three of those post-trained LLMs have themselves undergone an unknown degree of language drift from P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}, it is exceedingly unlikely that three distinct models have drifted to the same point in probability space. As such, we argue that by averaging over the three models, we can obtain a noisy triangulation of P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}.

Even with this instruct-model-derived approximation of P(HL){P^{(\textit{HL})}}, computing the full KL divergence between two LLMs is still intractable. We therefore measure relative language drift using CoT legibility as a proxy: the more an external reader is able to follow the CoT of an LLM, the less language drift that LLM has undergone.

Trace Legibility.

We implement an experimental design based on those used in Wang et al. (2025) and Roytburg et al. (2026). First, for each checkpoint π{\pi} selected after training in Section 5.1 (i.e. best-performing and iso-SFT/RLVR) and each prompt xx in the GSM8K validation set, we sample a reasoning trace and answer (z,y)∼π⁡(–|x)(z,y)\sim{\pi}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx). We then construct ten partial traces from zz, such that the nt​hn^{th} partial trace spans the first n/10n/10 of zz (see Figure 6).

For each partial trace, each of the three instruct models is prompted to guess the final answer yy, based on the reasoning produced by π{\pi} up to that point. By measuring the degree to which the instruct models are able to follow zz, this experiment provides an estimate of the legibility of the CoT—and therefore an estimate of the (lack of) language drift undergone by π{\pi}. We refer to this experiment as trace legibility.

As we are purely interested in CoT legibility, we do not measure final-answer correctness in this task, but rather final-answer agreement with the answer yy submitted by π{\pi}. In order to prevent the instruct models from simply ignoring the partial CoT and answering based solely on the question xx, we omit xx itself from the instruct models’ prompt: they are required to guess the final answer entirely from the fraction of the trace zz obtained from π{\pi}.

Self-Legibility.

We perform an additional round of trace legibility experiments, in which we replace the instruct-model CoT readers with other models of the same type and trained with the same method (SFT/RLVR) as π\pi. For example, if the target model π\pi is a Gemma model trained with RLVR, we replace the instruct models with the other four Gemma RLVR runs (i.e. the other four seeds). We refer to this experiment as self-legibility.

The goal of the self-legibility experiment is to measure the regularity (conversely, novelty) of language drift. If, for example, traces generated by an RLVR-trained model are more legible to other RLVR-trained models, we may conclude that RLVR-trained models tend to drift linguistically in the same direction in probability space. Conversely, if traces generated by an RLVR-trained model are less legible to other RLVR-trained models, then we may conclude that the direction of RLVR-induced language drift is unpredictable.

Additional details regarding the configuration of the trace legibility and self-legibility experiments are located in Appendix B.2.

CoT Utility Sanity Check.

For each training run, we confirm that the model is in fact utilizing its generated reasoning traces to produce final answers, rather than producing performative CoTs (Boppana et al., 2026), invisible reasoning (Baherwani et al., 2026), etc. A discussion of our methodology and results is located in Appendix C.

5.2 Results

GSM8K validation performance for each base, RLVR, and SFT model is given in Table 1. Recall that for the base models, we record accuracy with respect to both the last-submitted answer—used during training for validation and RLVR reward calculation—and the first-submitted answer, using the latter to estimate behavior-sharpening potential (see Section 5.1).

Qwen Undergoes Behavior Sharpening during RLVR.

The base Qwen model achieves an accuracy of ∼\sim0.61 when combining first-answer (0.41) and last-answer accuracy (0.20). Given that its final accuracy after RLVR is 0.79, we can conclude that around two-thirds of Qwen’s RLVR accuracy gains come purely from learning to emit the EOS token after submitting an answer.

This is not the case for Llama and Gemma: both models nearly triple their combined (first-answer plus last-answer) accuracy after RLVR. This is a clear indicator of novel behavior discovery. As such, we expect to see more pronounced language drift from RLVR for those models.

Novel Tasks Induce Language Drift.

In Figure 7, we plot for each model the difference between mean RLVR legibility and mean SFT legibility: values less than zero indicate that the SFT traces were more legible than the RLVR traces at that fraction. We expect the differences at earlier fractions to be near zero, as a final answer is extremely difficult to guess when given less than half of the corresponding trace, regardless of whether it was generated by RLVR- or SFT-trained models.

The plots in Figure 7 are summarized by the area-under-the-curve (AUC) values in Table 2. Llama and Gemma have negative values for trace legibility and self-legibility, both when comparing best-performing checkpoints and when comparing the training methods at iso-performance. This indicates that both models have higher degrees of language drift1111 11 We record anecdotal, qualitative examples of novel linguistic behavior from Llama and Gemma in Appendix D. across the board under RLVR, which is consistent with Theorems 1-2. That the Llama traces display higher degrees of language drift than Gemma is to be expected, as Gemma achieves much lower accuracy than Llama: when a task is too difficult, GRPO-style RL algorithms have very sparse gradients, and the LLM’s weights therefore cannot drift very far from those of the base model.

As predicted by the hypothesis in Section 4.3, Qwen—the only model that performs behavior sharpening during RLVR—is the only model for which RLVR exhibits virtually no language drift relative to SFT.

RLVR-Induced Language Drift is Unique.

The results of the self-legibility experiment indicate that the RLVR-trained Llama and Gemma models have a lower degree of mutual legibility than their SFT-trained counterparts. This indicates that each RLVR-trained run drifted in a different direction, which in turn indicates that each run developed unique linguistic behavior.

Conversely, Qwen—the only model that did not undergo RLVR-induced language drift as measured by trace legibility—is the only model type for which the RLVR-trained models have a higher degree of mutual legibility than the SFT-trained models.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

In this paper, we presented evidence that RLVR on novel tasks induces language drift in LLMs. In Section 4, we proved theoretically that there is a finite upper bound on the maximum possible language drift that can occur during SFT, while no such upper bound exists for RLVR. Furthermore, we proved that language drift cannot be constrained during RLVR training without constraining expected reward (Theorem 3).

We then demonstrated empirically that LLMs undergo a greater degree of language drift under RLVR than under SFT, when behavior sharpening is not viable—i.e. when the task is novel to the base model (Section 5). We furthermore showed that such RLVR-induced drift is unique, in that models of the same type trained on different seeds suffer from decreased mutual legibility.

The implications of these findings with respect to frontier-model CoT monitorability are considerable. In particular, the conditions under which RLVR induces language drift—novel reasoning tasks—are precisely those under which models must be trained in order to advance the frontier. Furthermore, these are precisely the conditions under which RLVR is most needed, due to the difficulty of obtaining sufficient amounts of SFT data on novel reasoning environments.

It then follows from Theorem 3 that we must accept increasing degrees of language drift in order to continue advancing the frontier with RLVR. Finally, that RLVR-induced language drift is unique—even among models initialized from the same base and trained on the same task—indicates that it is unpredictable: a given model can drift linguistically in multiple possible directions during RLVR training. This suggests that even a model trained on the same data as some target model π{\pi} cannot necessarily be relied upon to effectively comprehend—and therefore, monitor—the internal reasoning traces produced by π{\pi}.

Limitations

Due to resource constraints, we used only small, 1-1.5B models in our experiments. The use of such models naturally limits the size and difficulty of the reasoning datasets that they can be trained on: while we undeniably observe language drift in the Llama and Gemma models (see Appendix D), this drift does not reach the degree of illegibility displayed in some frontier-model internal reasoning traces (e.g. in Figure 3).

Due to the restricted range of datasets that these small models can be trained on, we were only able to find one dataset (GSM8K) that both contained annotated CoTs and that could be learned through RLVR and SFT by the three base models (Llama, Gemma, and Qwen; see Section 5.1). In future versions of this manuscript, we intend to extend the results of our experiments in Section 5 with additional reasoning datasets.

Finally, our experiments in Section 5 primarily pertain to Theorems 1-2 and our hypothesis in Section 4.3: we do not include any empirical demonstration of our theoretical findings in Section 4.2 (Theorem 3) that constraining language drift necessarily constrains expected reward. We likewise intend to update future versions of the manuscript with experiments to this end.

A.3 Theorem 3

Let π∗\pi^{*} be any conditional distribution over 𝒵×𝒴\mathcal{Z}\times\mathcal{Y} given 𝒳\mathcal{X} such that:

∀x:∑z∈𝒵π∗​(z,y∗​(x)|x)=1\forall x\colon\sum_{z\in\mathcal{Z}}\pi^{*}(z,y^{*}(x)\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx)=1 (15)

Where y∗​(x)=argmaxy⁡D(RL)​(y|x)y^{*}(x)=\operatorname{argmax}_{y}{{D}^{(\textit{RL})}}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx). By assumption (Section 3.3) and definition, P(HL)​(z,y|x)≠0{P^{(\textit{HL})}}(z,y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx)\neq 0 and π∗​(z,y|x)=0\pi^{*}(z,y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx)=0: therefore, DKL(P(HL)(–|x)||π∗(–|x))=∞D_{\textit{KL}}({P^{(\textit{HL})}}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx)\hskip 2.84526pt||\hskip 2.84526pt\pi^{*}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx))=\infty.

Now, for any 0≤ϵ<∞0\leq\epsilon<\infty, define πϵ\pi_{\epsilon} as in Equation 16:

πϵ=argmaxπ∈ℬ⁡(ϵ)​ℛ​(D(RL),π)\pi_{\epsilon}=\underset{\pi\in\mathcal{B}(\epsilon)}{\operatorname{argmax}}\hskip 2.84526pt{\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},\pi) (16)

For any 0<λ<10<\lambda<1, ℛ⁡(D(RL),πϵ(λ))=λ⋅ℛ⁡(D(RL),π∗)+(1−λ)⋅ℛ⁡(D(RL),πϵ){\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},\pi^{(\lambda)}_{\epsilon})=\lambda\cdot{\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},\pi^{*})+(1-\lambda)\cdot{\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},\pi_{\epsilon}) by construction, and therefore ℛ⁡(D(RL),πϵ(λ))>ℛ⁡(D(RL),πϵ){\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},\pi^{(\lambda)}_{\epsilon})>{\mathcal{R}}({{D}^{(\textit{RL})}},\pi_{\epsilon}). Appendix B Experimental Methodology

B.1 Training and Validation

For each model and training type, we performed a hyperparameter grid search across the values given in Table 3: DAPO required a large group size due to the low success probabilities of the base models. All models were trained with a cosine learning rate scheduler with a warmup ratio of 0.03, using the few-shot prompt in Figure 8. For the DAPO training runs, we fixed the number of update iterations (μ\mu) at 1, ϵlow\epsilon_{\textit{low}} at 0.2, and ϵhigh\epsilon_{\textit{high}} at 0.28.

Each training run was performed on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU.

B.2 Trace Legibility

In the trace legibility task, all instruct models were prompted using the prompt in Figure 11, and in the self-legibility task, all models were prompted using the prompt in Figure 10. Sampling for all models—generators and readers—was carried out deterministically.

Appendix C CoT Utility Sanity Check

C.1 Performative CoT

We first verified that the models were not generating performative CoTs: i.e. determining the answer early on, and simply generating a CoT post-hoc to mimic their training distribution (Boppana et al., 2026).

Recall that in the trace legibility experiment in Section 5.1.2, we sampled for each query xx a trace/answer pair (z,y)∼π⁡(–|x)(z,y)\sim{\pi}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx), then split zz into a sequence of partial traces z0.0,…,z0.9z_{0.0},\dots,z_{0.9}. In the present experiment, we measured the probability π⁡(y|x,zn){\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z_{n}) of the answer yy conditioned on each partial trace znz_{n}, and compared it to the probability π⁡(y|x,z){\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z) of yy given the full trace zz: if π\pi is generating performative CoTs, we would expect π⁡(y|x,zn)≈π⁡(y|x,z){\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z_{n})\approx{\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z). On the other hand, if π\pi is actually using the full reasoning trace, we would expect π⁡(y|x,zn)≪π⁡(y|x,z){\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z_{n})\ll{\pi}(y\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx,z).

In Figure 12, we plot the mean (over all queries xx) difference in final-answer probability conditioned on partial traces compared to final-answer probability conditioned on full traces. Across nearly all models and seeds—with the exception of Gemma Iso-SFT—we see final-answer probability increasing as the partial trace fraction approaches 1, indicating that the models are in fact using their CoTs.

C.2 Invisible Reasoning

Next, we verified that the models were not performing invisible reasoning: simply using the CoT to perform computations in the hidden states to arrive at the final answer, independently of the actual tokens in the CoT (Baherwani et al., 2026).

In this experiment, we collected the 128 trace/answer pairs (zi,yi)∼π⁡(–|xi)(z_{i},y_{i})\sim{\pi}(\text{\textendash}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i}), and bucketed the reasoning traces by length. The traces were placed into ten buckets: one for each decile.

For each query/trace/answer triple (xi,zi,yi)(x_{i},z_{i},y_{i}), we computed the final-answer probability π⁡(yi|xi,zk){\pi}(y_{i}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i},z_{k}) conditioned on five zkz_{k} from the same length bucket as ziz_{i} (ensuring that k≠ik\neq i), and compared these probabilities to the original π⁡(yi|xi,zi){\pi}(y_{i}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i},z_{i}). If π{\pi} is performing invisible reasoning, we would expect that the actual tokens in the reasoning chain do not impact final-answer probability. Otherwise, we would expect that the probability of yiy_{i} conditioned on a reasoning trace zkz_{k}—generated for a different query xkx_{k}—would be significantly lower than conditioned on the original trace ziz_{i}: π⁡(yi|xi,zk)≪π⁡(yi|xi,zi){\pi}(y_{i}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i},z_{k})\ll{\pi}(y_{i}\hskip 2.84526pt|\hskip 2.84526ptx_{i},z_{i}).

In Table 4, we report the mean difference between original answer probability and swapped answer probability: this value is positive for all models, indicating that they are not performing invisible reasoning in their CoTs.
